course.title: Neural scaling laws, from power laws to compute-optimal training
course.level: curious beginner; assumes logarithms and the idea of a power law
course.license: Example review shipped with the course-to-shorts repository (examples/reviews/scaling-laws/review.md); cited papers fetched from arXiv

units.title: Error falls as a power law
units.summary: Across translation, language modelling, image classification and speech, generalisation error falls as a power law in training-set size, so learning curves are straight lines on log-log axes and small runs predict large ones; Rosenfeld et al. fit one functional form in both model and data size.
key_ideas: joint form in model and data size

units.title: Language models: bigger models, stopped early
units.summary: Kaplan et al. find Transformer test loss follows power laws in non-embedding parameters (0.076), data (0.095) and compute (0.050); their compute-efficient allocation grows the model as C^0.73 and the data only as C^0.27, so large models should be stopped well before convergence.

units.title: Compute-optimal training: scale data with the model
units.summary: Hoffmann et al. refit the allocation with over 400 models and three methods, finding parameters and tokens should grow about equally (N_opt ~ C^0.5); Chinchilla (70B params, 1.4T tokens) used Gopher's budget (280B, 300B) and beat it, about 20 tokens per parameter.

units.title: Checking and reconciling the fits
units.summary: Besiroglu et al. refit Hoffmann's third method and find the published fit inconsistent, with the corrected fit agreeing with equal scaling; Pearce and Song show that counting only non-embedding parameters at small scale biases the Chinchilla analysis to about 0.78, close to Kaplan's 0.73.

units.title: Beyond training compute
units.summary: Sardana et al. add inference cost: when a model will serve many requests, a smaller model trained on more tokens than the Chinchilla ratio minimises total cost.
